g A successor or succession to continue for ever in his family, as this phrase is expounded 1 Kings 11. 36. & 15. 4. and particularly one eminent and glorious light, to wit, the Messias, who shall come out of his loyns, and revive and vastly enlarge his Kingdom.

entries.title: Psalms 132:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
h For the shameful and unexpected disappointment of all their vain hopes and wicked designs.

i Upon him and his posterity, which are nothing else but a mans self multiplied.

entries.title: Psalms 133:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a You have been harassed by a Civil War, take notice of this blessed change with thankfulness to God for it.

b For us who are brethren not onely by nature and blood, but also by combination in one and the same Commonwealth, and by the profession of the same Religion.

Heb. [illegible] together.

entries.title: Psalms 133:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Exod. 30. 25, 30.

c It is no less grateful and refreshing than that oyl which was plentifully poured forth upon Aarons head at the time of his Consecration to the Priestly Office, which was exceeding pleasant, not onely for the extraordinary fragrancy of it, but because by this, together with the other Rites prescribed, he was initiated into that sacred Office, which was so acceptable to God, and so comfortable and beneficial to the people, as being the happy instrument of making atonement to God for them, and of procuring and maintaining their peace with God, upon which all their happiness of this life and of the next depends.

Or, [illegible]ollar.

d Or, skirt, for the Hebrew word is of the Singular number. Not to the lower skirt or bottom of his Sacerdotal garment, for that the sacred Oyl was poured forth in so great plenty is not probable, nor was it necessary or convenient; but to the upper skirt of it, or the mouth of it, as this Hebrew word properly signifies, or to the coll[illegible]r of his upper Priestly garment, which the oyntment falling upon his beard, might easily reach.

entries.title: Psalms 133:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 4. 48. [illegible], [illegible].

e It is no less grateful than the dew is which f[illegible]lls upon that great and goodly hill of Hermon, whereby it is both refreshed and made fruitful.

[illegible]. 25. 21.

f And as the dew which falle[illegible]h upon the mountains of Sion, i. e. either upon the several parts and ridges or tops of that mountain, whereof one was peculiarly called Sion, and another Moriah; or upon the mountains which are round about Ierusalem, Psal. 125. 2. which is oft called Zion, as Psal. 132. 13. And these may be opposed to Hermon, which was remote and beyond Iordan. But peradventure (which yet I propose with all submission) this dew is not to be taken literally, for the falling of the dew availed very little to the refreshment or improvement of the hills of Sion and Moriah, especially as now they were filled with buildings, but Allegorically, for the favour or blessing of God, which is frequently called and compared to the dew, as Prov. 19. 12. Isa. 18. 4. Hos. 14. 5. Mich. 5. 7. And thus it may seem to be explained in the following clause: and so the sence of the place is this, It is as desirable as the natural dew which falls upon mount Hermon, nay which is more, as that blessed and heavenly dew of Gods ordinances and graces which he hath commanded to fall upon the mountains of Sion, i. e. either upon mount Sion, the Plural number being put for the Singular, as it is Psal. 132. 7. and oft elsewhere, as I have observed in several places; or upon the mountains of Zion and Moriah, and others which are round about Ierusalem, as was now said. And if it seem strange, that the dew should be taken literally in the first clause, and mystically in the next, we have a like instance Mat. 8. 22. Let the dead (spiritually) bury the dead (naturally.)

g He now gives the reason either why this unity is so good a thing; or why the dew descending upon Zion, to which that is compared, is so desirable. And so upon this occasion he slides into the commendation of Zions felicity, as the sacred Writers frequently do upon other like occasions

[illegible]. 28. 8.

h Either, 1. where brethren live in peace and unity: or rather, 2. in Zion last mentioned.

i Ordained, promised, conferred and established his blessing, to wit, all manner of blessedness for his people that since[illegible]ely worship him in that place.

k To wit, an happy and pleasant life; for to live in misery is accounted and oft called death both in Scripture and in other Authors.

entries.title: Psalms 134:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Do not stand there like statues, dumb and idle, but employ your hearts and tongues in singing forth the praises of the Lord.

b Peculiarly so called, Priests and Levites, who are set apart to the service of God and of the Sanctuary, as the next clause restrains this general expression.

[illegible] Chr. 9. 33.

c Not onely by day, but also and especially by night, when their watch was more necessary. See Exod. 27. 21. Levit. 8. 35. 1 Sam. 3. 3. As you watch by night when others sleep, so do you utter the praises of God when others are silent.

d i. e. Serve or minister, as this word is used Deut. 10. 8. & 18. 7. and oft elsewhere.

e Which word includes both the Temple and Courts belonging to it, as hath been noted before.

entries.title: Psalms 134:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f Unto God in prayer and praises, thus expressing and exciting your inward devotion.

[illegible], in holiness.

g In that holy house of God where you stand, v. 1. Or, in or with holiness: Lift up your hands, as it is prescribed, 1 Tim. 2. 8. Do not content your selves with lifting up your hands, but see that this be done with pure and holy hearts.

entries.title: Psalms 134:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
h Either, 1. thee whosoever thou ar[illegible] who dost faithfully perform the duty here commanded. Or, 2. thee, O King, or Priest, who dost engage and encourage us in this blessed work.

i Where God dwells, and from whence he heareth the prayers of his people, and giveth them the blessings which they desire and need.

entries.title: Psalms 135:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: a Ye Priests and Levites, as Psal. 134. 1.

entries.title: Psalms 135:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: b Either in the Temple or the inner Court, which were appropriated to the Priests and Levites; or in the outward Court, which was for the people. See 2 Chron. 4. 9.

entries.title: Psalms 135:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
c Bountiful and gracious, especially to you, and therefore he justly expects and deserves your praises.

d The work it self of singing praises to God is pleasant, as it is more fully expressed, Psal. 147. 1.

entries.title: Psalms 135:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 95. 3.

e Above all that are called Gods, or worshipped as Gods by the heathen people. And therefore seeing they commonly praise and extol their Idols, it becometh you not to be silent as to the praises of your God.

entries.title: Psalms 135:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 115. 3.

f Either in the creation or government of them.

g His power and juri[illegible]diction is universal, and not like that of the heathen Gods, which is confined to their several Countries.

Heb. depths.

h In the visible Seas, and in those invisible depths both of earth and of the waters which are contained in the bowels of the earth.

entries.title: Psalms 135:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Jer. 10. 13. & 51. 16[illegible]

Gr. clouds. So Prov. 25. 14.

i Which are the matter of clouds and rain.

k Either, 1. from the Sea, the common source of vapors, 1 Kings 18. 44. Amos 5. 8. wherewith both the earth in general, and several particular countries, are terminated or bounded: o[illegible] rather, 2. from all parts of the earth from one end to another, as the borders of a land are commonly put for the whole land from one border to another, as Psal. 105. 31, 33. & 147. 14. and oft elsewhere. For in this sence this phrase is generally used in Scripture, as Iob 28. 24. & 38. 13. Psal. 19. 4, 6. & 48. 10. and every where.

Job 38. 24 &c. Zech. 10. 1.

l He bringeth water even out of the fire: he maketh thick clouds, which being broken, produce lightnings, and so are dissolved into showers of rain. So the lightnings are both a sign and in some sort the cause of rain. Or, he maketh lightnings with (as this Particle is used Gen. 46. 26. Psal. 89. 4. & 119. 56, 98.) rain, i. e. he causeth both of them to come out of the same cloud.

m Out of those secret places where he reserves them, and whence he bringeth them, as he sees fit. Thus we read of treasures of snow and hail, Iob 38. 22. not that they are formally laid up in any certain places, but to signifie that God hath them as much at his disposal as any man hath th[illegible] which he hath laid up in his stores.

entries.title: Psalms 135:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Exod. 12. 12, 29.

n From the general works of Nature he comes to Gods special works of Providence towards his people.

Heb. from man unto beast.

entries.title: Psalms 135:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 102. 12.

Heb. to generation and generation.

o These wonderful works of thine shall never be forgotten. The land which thou gavest us, v. 12. and which we yet enjoy, is an everlasting monument of thy power and goodness, and an obligation and encouragement to trust in thee in all our present or future difficulties.

entries.title: Psalms 135:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
p Will in due time plead the cause of his people, or give judgment for them, as this phrase is used Deut. 32. 36. Ier. 5. 28 & 22. 16.

q He will recal that severe sentence which for their sins he had passed upon them, and be reconciled to them.

entries.title: Psalms 135:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 115. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.

r Of this and the following verses see the Notes on Psal. 115. 4, 5, &c.

entries.title: Psalms 135:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: Heb. let them be. So Gr.

entries.title: Psalms 135:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
s By the assemblies of his people in Zion or Ierusalem.

t This clause may be added either to distinguish the true God from the gods which were worshipped in other places and countries; or as a reason why they should bless God, because he had blessed and honoured that place with his gracious and glorious presence.

entries.title: Psalms 136:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Deut. 10. 17.

a Who is infinitely superiour to all that are called gods, whether Angels, or Princes, or Idols.

entries.title: Psalms 136:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: b He and none else. Or, he without the help of any other person or thing, whereas no other being can do any thing alone or without his help.

entries.title: Psalms 136:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Gen. 1. 1.

c To wit, by eminent and admirable wisdom, far exceeding the capacity of all humane or Angelical creatures.

entries.title: Psalms 136:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Gen. 1. 9. Je[illegible]. 10. 12.

d Of which see on Gen. 1. 9. Psal. 24. 2.

entries.title: Psalms 136:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. for the [illegible]lings by day.

e Of which phrase and the like in the next verse, see my Notes on Gen. 1. 16.

entries.title: Psalms 136:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: f To wit, without fear or danger, by comparing this with the next verse.

entries.title: Psalms 136:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Exod. 14. 28.

Heb. shaked off.

entries.title: Psalms 136:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Exod. 15. 22.

g Through that vast howling wilderness where there was neither way nor provision; through which none but the Almighty God could have safely conducted them.

entries.title: Psalms 136:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: h He speaks of all that people as of one man, because they were united together in one body in the worship of one and the same God. Thus God calleth them all his first-born, Exod. 4. 22.

entries.title: Psalms 136:25
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 104. 27. & 147. 9.

i Either to all mankind: or to all living creatures. For which God deserves great praises, which the Psalmist by his example teacheth us to render to God for them, because those who are most concerned either cannot or do not perform this duty.

entries.title: Psalms 137:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Either, 1. of the City of Babylon, and then the river is Euphrates here called rivers for its greatness, and by a common Enallage of the Plural for the Singular, as Tigris also is, Nah. 2. 6. yea and Iordan, Psal. 74. 15. Or, 2. of the Territory of Babylon, in which there were many rivers, as Euphrates, which also was divided into several streams or rivule[illegible]s, and Tigris and others. Here they were either by the appointment of their Lords for the making or repairing of the works beside the river: or by choice, retiring themselves thither from the noise and observation of their enemies, as they had opportunity, that they might disburden their oppressed minds before the Lord.

b The usual posture of mourners, Ezra 9. 4, &c. Iob 2. 12. Isa. 47. 1, 5.

c Either, 1. our former enjoyments in Zion, which greatly aggravated their present misery, Lam. 1. 7. Or, 2. Zions present desolations and pollutions.

entries.title: Psalms 137:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d These are not without great probability supposed to be the words of some holy Levites, who had been accustomed to musick, both vocal and instrumental, in the service of the Temple. Harps are here put by a Synecdoche for all instruments of musick. It is further to be observed, That although the harp was used by the Grecians in mourning, yet it was used by the Hebrews in re[illegible]oycing, as is manifest from Gen. 31. 27. 2 Chron. 20. 27, 28. Psal. 43. 4, &c. This passage is to be understood either, 1. figuratively, signifying onely that they abandoned all signs and means of comfort: or rather, 2. properly, as the following songs are, which the Babylonians required them to sing to their harps And these harps they might either, 1. bring from Ierusalem, which they might desire to do to preserve those sacred utensils, and their enemies might either permit or command them to do for their own delight: or, 2. procure in Babylon, that they might sometimes solace themselves with the practice of some of the Temple-musick, which they desired and intended to do; but when they came to the tryal, they were not able to do it, and therefore laid them by.

e Which commonly grow upon the banks of rivers, as they did by Euphrates in such plenty, that from thence it is called the brook of willows, Isa. 15. 7.

entries.title: Psalms 137:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] word [illegible].

[illegible] laid us [illegible].

[illegible] 79. 1.

f Such songs as you used to sing in the Temple at Sion. Which they required either out of curiosity, or to delight their ears, or rather by way of scoffing and insultation over them and their Temple and Religion.

entries.title: Psalms 137:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g Those songs which were appointed by God, and to be sung onely to his honour and in his service.

[illegible] land of [illegible].

h When we are banished from our own Temple and Land, and amongst those who are strangers and enemies to God and to his Worship? So we should prostitute and [illegible]rofane Gods Ordinances. And this answer they either expressed to their enemies, or kept in their own breasts when they refused to comply with their desire.

entries.title: Psalms 137:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i If I do not retain a deep and sorrowful sence of thy ruine and misery, or if I [illegible]dulge my self in mirth and jollity, as if I had forgotten thee.

k The chief instrument of playing upon musical instruments and of other actions.

l i. e. Lose its skill of playing. In the Hebrew it is onely, forget, without expressing what, to intimate the extent and generality of this wish, Let it forget or be disenabled not onely for playing, but for every action in which it was formerly used.

entries.title: Psalms 137:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m With affection and sympathy, so as to damp my joys.

n Be made uncapable of singing or speaking or [illegible]oving, as it is in some diseases. Compare Iob 29. 10 Psal. 22. 16.

[illegible]eb. the [illegible]ad [illegible] [illegible].

o If I do not value and desire Ierusalems prosperity more than all other delights, and consequently if Ierusalems misery doth not so deeply affect me as to hinder my delight in all other things.

entries.title: Psalms 137:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
p So as to punish them.

[illegible]. 49. 7. [illegible]. 25. 12.

q Our constant and inveterate enemies, who had no regard either to consanguinity or humanity

r In the time of its calamity or destruction, which is oft called a day, as Iob 18. 20. Psal. 37. 13. Ezek. 30. 9. Hos. 11. 11. Obad. v. 12.

s To the Babylonians, whom they assisted and provoked against Ierusalem: of which see Lam. 4. 11. Ezek. 25. 12. Obad. v. 11, 12, 13, 14.

[illegible]. 10. &c. [illegible] make [illegible].

entries.title: Psalms 137:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t By which he understands the City and Empire of Babylo[illegible] and the people thereof.

Heb. wasted.

u Who art by Gods righteous and irrevocable Sentence devoted to certain destruction.

x As being Gods instrument to vindicate his honour, and execute his just judgments, and fulfil his counsel and word: which Cyr[illegible]s was to his own great glory and advantage, as appears both from sacred and profane History.

Heb. that r[illegible] compenseth unto thee thy deed which thou didst to us.

Jer. 50. 15, 29. Rev. 18. 6.

y That shall use thee with equal cruelty.

entries.title: Psalms 137:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Isa. 13. 16.

Heb. the rock.

z As thou didst use our little ones. So this was but a just re[illegible]ation foretold here, as also Is[illegible]. 13. 16.

entries.title: Psalms 138:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 119. 46. Gr. before Angels.

a Either, 1. before the Angels, who were represented by the Cherubims upon the Ark, who are called Gods, Psal. 8. 6. & 97. 7. Comp. with Heb. 1. 6. & 2. 7. who also are present in the congregations of Gods people[illegible], 1 Cor 11. 10. Or rather, 2. before Kings and Princes, by comparing this with v. 4. All Kings (provoked by my example) shall praise thee; and with Psal. 119. 46. I will speak of thy te[illegible]monies before kings. And these are most commonly called Gods in Scripture, as Exod. 21. 6. & 23. 9, 28. comp. with Deut. 19. 17. Besides, David mentions this as something singular and extraordinary, and designed by him, whereas the doing of this before the Angels is common to all, and is unavoidably necessary.

entries.title: Psalms 138:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
b Where the Ark was. He saith towards it, because he was not permitted to enter into it.

c For thou hast glorified thy word or promise or thy faithfulness in fulfil[illegible]ing thy promises to me more than any other of thy glorious perfections by which thou ar[illegible] known. Not that one of Gods Attributes is really and in it self more great or glorious than another, or can be made so, but because one may be more celebrated and admi[illegible]ed by men than another, as here Gods gracious promise made [illegible]o David, and the wonderful accomplishment thereof in spight of all those difficulties which stood in the way, and which seemed to men to be insuperable, was at this time more observed and admired than any other of his Attributes or actions. But here we must remember, that amongst the rest of the promises made to David, one was that the Messias should come out of his loyns, and that those parts of the promised mercies which David had actually received, were pledges to assure him that he should receive the rest in due [illegible]ime, and especially that great and eminent word of promise concerning the Mess[illegible]s, which might well be said to be magnified above all Gods name.

entries.title: Psalms 138:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: d This last clause limits and explains the former, how God answered him so speedily, not by giving him the thing which he desired in that very instant, but by giving him inward support and patience to wa[illegible]t Gods time, and to [illegible]ear all his troubles chearfully in the mean time, which was a singular mercy, and indeed greater than the actual don[illegible] of any temporal blessing.

entries.title: Psalms 138:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
e Either, 1. all neighbouring Kings: or, 2. the g[illegible]rality of Kings and Princes upon earth. And so this is a Prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles. Which seems to be co[illegible] firmed by the next verse, which expresseth their extraordinary joy and a[illegible] e[illegible]inent advancement of Gods glory, which agrees much better to this great occasion, than to that of Davids exaltation to the Throne, wherein the other Kings of the earth were not much concerned.

f Either, 1. thy promises declared unto them by me: or, 2. the Gospel preached among them.

entries.title: Psalms 138:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g Or, of, or, for or because of the ways of the Lord, i. e. his wonderful counsel and gracious providences towards themselves and others.

h Or, great shall be. At that time the worship and glory of God shall not be confined to one small land as now it is, but shall be extended to all the parts of the world.

entries.title: Psalms 138:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 113. 5, 6. Isa[illegible]. 57. 15.

Heb. he seeth

Jam. 4. 6. 1 Pet. 5. 5.

i Unto such as are mean and obscure in the world, to me a poor contemptible shepherd, whom he hath preferred before great Princes, and to such as are little in their own eyes.

Or, and.

k But as for the great men of the world, who are lifted up in pride, he looks upon them as they do upon others, with s[illegible]orn and contempt, and at a great distance, as disdaining to admit them into his presence. But the words may be, and by divers Interpreters are rendred otherwise, And he who is high or the lo[illegible]ty one from afar (i. e. from his high and holy place, even the highest Heavens where he dwells, notwithstanding that distance) doth know them, or will owne them. So this is the repetition of the former sentence, as is very usual in this Book. And this seems best to suit as with the [illegible]oregoing, so also with the following words, and thus all will be understood of one and the same sort of persons.

entries.title: Psalms 138:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
l i. e. Be encompassed with dangers.

m Thou wilt chear my spirit and preserve my life.

n Put forth thy Almighty power.

o To oppose and restrain their rage, and to save me from them, as it follows.

entries.title: Psalms 138:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 57. 2. Phil. 1. 6.

Or, for me.

p Will finish that great work of my deliverance and advancement, which he hath undertaken and carried on hitherto.

q It is not inconstant and changeable, as mens affections are, but everlasting. And this may be either a proof of the foregoing assertion, the Lord will perfect, &c. or an argument to enforce the following petition, therefore forsake not, &c.

r Or, leave not, or, do not desist from or give over.

s The work of my salvation which is thus far advanced, not by any humane help, but by thine own extraordinary power and providence, and therefore it is not for thine honour to desert it at last. This he calls works in regard of the many and various parts and actions which concurred to this work.

entries.title: Psalms 139:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: a i. e. Known me exactly, as men do those things which they di[illegible]gently search out.

entries.title: Psalms 139:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
b All my postures and motions, my actions and my cessations from action.

c All my secret counsels and designs.

d Before they are perfectly formed in my mind. Thou knowest what my thoughts will be i[illegible] such and such circumstances, long before I know it, yea from all eternity.

entries.title: Psalms 139:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, win[illegible]owest.

e Thou watchest me on every side, and therefore discernest every step which I take. It is a Metaphor either from huntsmen watching all the motions and lurking places of wild beasts, that they may catch them; or from Souldiers be[illegible]ieging their enemies in a City, and setting watches round about them.

f Me when I lye down in my bed, where men oft contrive what they execute in the day time.

entries.title: Psalms 139:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: g Thou knowest what I speak, and with what design and disposition of mind. Or rather, as others render it, and which is more admirable, When there is not a word, &c. Thou knowest what I intend to speak either in prayer to thee, or in conversation with men, when I have not yet uttered one word of it.

entries.title: Psalms 139:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
h With thine all-seeing and all-disposing Providence.

i Thou keepest me, as it were with a strong hand, in thy sight and under thy power.

entries.title: Psalms 139:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 131. 1.

k I am so far from equalling thy knowledge, that I cannot apprehend it, in what manner thou dost so perfectly know all things, even such as are most secret and have yet no being, and seem to depend upon many casualties and uncertainties.

entries.title: Psalms 139:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Jer. 23. 24.

l Either, 1. from the Holy Ghost, the third Person in the Trinity: or, 2. from thee who art a Spirit, and therefore canst penetrate into the most secret parts: or, 3. from thy mind or understanding, of which he is here speaking, as this word seems to be taken, Isa. 40. 13. compared with Rom. 11. 34. for what there is called the Spirit of the Lord, is here called the mind of the Lord. And as the Spirit of God is oft used in Scripture for its gifts and graces, so the Spirit of God in this place may be put for that knowledge which is an Attribute or action of God.

Heb. thy [illegible]ace. So G[illegible].

m A man can go to no place which is out of thy sight.

entries.title: Psalms 139:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Am. 9. 2, 3, 4.

Prov. 15. 11.

n If I should or could repose and hide my self in the grave or in the lowest parts of the earth, which are at the farthest distance from Heaven.

entries.title: Psalms 139:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: o If I should flee as swiftly from thy presence as the morning light doth, which in an instant scat[illegible]ereth it self from East to West: for the Sea being the Western border of [illegible]anaan, is oft put for the West in Scripture. And wings are Poetically ascribed to the morning or morning light here, as they are elsewhere to the Sun, as Mal. 4. 2. and to the winds, as Psal. 18. 11. & 104. 3. and to other things of eminent swiftness.

entries.title: Psalms 139:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: p I could neither go thither without thy conduct, nor subsist there without thy powerful support, and much less could I go out of thy sight; for a man may see many things which are out of his power.

entries.title: Psalms 139:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: q Shall be as clear and manifest to God as the light it self.

entries.title: Psalms 139:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Job 26. 6. & 34. 22. Heb. 4. 1[illegible].

Heb. darkneth not.

r Or, enlightneth, as this word is used Psal. 19. 9. Prov. 29. 13, &c. discovereth me and all mine actions.

Heb. as is [illegible] darkness, so is the light.

s This is repeated so oft to reprove and confute the ridiculous conceits of many ungodly men, who flatter themselves with hopes of secrecy and impunity for those sins which they commit in the dark. See Isa. 29. 15.

entries.title: Psalms 139:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t Or, thou dost possess, thou dwellest in them, thou art the Owner and Governor of them, and therefore must needs know them. Or, thou hast formed, as some of the Ancients and others render it.

u The most inward and hidden part of the body, supposed also to be the seat of mens lusts and passions.

x Either, 1. with that covering called the afterbirth, wherein the infant is wrapped and preserved in the womb by the wonderful care of Divine providence. Or, 2. with skin and flesh, as it is expressed Iob 10. 11.

entries.title: Psalms 139:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. by [illegible] things I a[illegible] become [illegible].

y Thy infinite wisdom and power manifested in the rare and curious structure of mans body, doth fill me with wonder and astonishment and with the dread of thy Majesty.

z Both in the lesser world, man, and in the greater.

Heb. greatly.

a I am well assured both by thy word and by the contemplation and study of thy works, to which I have much addicted my self, that they are wonderful, although I do not so accurately understand all the particulars of them as I would do.

entries.title: Psalms 139:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Job 10. 8, 10. Eccl. 11. 5.

Or, strength, [illegible], [illegible].

b Or, My bone, as the LXX and others render the word. And bone may be here taken collectively for bones, as is usual in such words, or for the whole fabrick of the bones. And the bones may be very fitly mentioned here, because they are inward and invisible, as being covered with skin and flesh and sinews. Or, the bones may be put Synecdochically for the whole body, as being the most substantial part of it, as they are Psal. 35. 10.

c In the dark vault of my mothers womb.

d Heb. embroidered, exquisitely composed of bones and muscles and sinews and veins and arteries and other parts, all framed with such wonderful skill, that even Heathens upon the contemplation of all the parts of mans body, and how excellently they were framed both for beauty and use, have broken forth into pangs of admiration and adoration of the Creator of man, as Galen particularly did

e Or, as it were in the lowest parts of the earth. So there is onely an Ellipsis of the note of similitude, which is very frequent in Scripture, as hath been often said and proved. In a place as secret and remote from humane eyes, as the lowest parts of the earth are, to wit, in my mothers womb. And so what was said in the former clause is repeated in this in other words.

entries.title: Psalms 139:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f When I was a meer Embryo, a rude and shapeless lump, when I was first conceived.

g In thy counsel and providence, by which thou didst co[illegible]trive and effect this great work and all the parts of it according to that model which thou hadst appointed. This is a M[illegible]taphor taken from workmen, who when they are to make some curious structure, they first draw a rude draught or delineation of it, by which they govern themselves in the building of it.

Heb. all of [illegible]

h All the several parts of my substance.

Or, what days [illegible] should be [illegible]ed.

i Which in due time and by degrees were formed into bones, fleshy sinews, &c. Or, as it is in the margent, what days (and the days in which) they wer[illegible] or should be fashioned, by what steps, in what order and time each part of the body should receive its proper form. This also was written or appointed by God.

k Heb. and not one of them, understand either yet was, as it is in our Translation; or, was lacking, to wit, in thy book. All my parts without exception were written by thee. But then these words are not to be joyned with those immediately foregoing, but with the former, and the words are to be read thus, in thy book all my mem[illegible]ers were written (which in continuance were fashioned) when as yet, &c.

entries.title: Psalms 139:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 40. 5.

l Thy is taken either, 1. passively, my thoughts of thee: or rather, 2. actively, thy thoughts, counse[illegible]s or cont[illegible]ivances on my behalf, which are admirable and am[illegible]able in mine eyes. Thou didst not onely form me at first, but ev[illegible] [illegible]ince my conception and birth thy thoughts have been employed for me in preserving and providing for me and blessing of me.

m Thy gracious designs and providences towards me are numberless, as it follows.

entries.title: Psalms 139:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: n To wit, by my thoughts and meditations. Thy wonderful counsels and works on my behalf come constantly into my mind, not onely in the day time, but even in the night season, which is commonly devoted to rest and sleep, whensoever I awake either in the night or in the morning: These are my last thoughts when I lye down, and my first when I rise.

entries.title: Psalms 139:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o And as thou hast precious and gracious thoughts towards me and all that love and fear thee, so thou hast other kinds of thoughts and purposes towards wicked men, such as thou knowest mine enemies to be, even to destroy them utterly.

p I renounce your friendship and society. I will not partake with you in your sins, lest I should also partake of your plagues.

q Heb. ye men of blood, either, 1. passively, deserving death, or guilty of blood or of death, as the phrase is, Numb. 35. 27, 31. Mat. 26. 66. Or rather, 2. actively, blood-thirsty, or shedders of blood, as this phrase is generally taken, as 2 Sam. 16. 8. Psal. 26. 9. & 55. 24. & 59. 3. Having called them wicked men in general, he now gives a particular account of their wickedness, they were unjust and cruel towards men, and withal profane and impious towards God, as he tells us in the next verse.

entries.title: Psalms 139:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. speak of thee in wickedness, or, unto wickedness.

r By profane scoffs, and a professed den[illegible]al or contempt of thine Omniscience and Providence. Or, they speak of thee in or unto wickedness, they make use of Religion to cover or further their wicked designs. But our Translation is more favoured by the Context, which speaks of Gods open and professed enemies.

s Or, according to the order of the Hebrew words, and take thy Name in vain, and are thine enemies, or haters of thee, as it follows v. 20. These words, thy Name, are understood here, as also Isa. 3. 7. out of Exod. 20. 7. where they are expressed. They abuse thy blessed Name with hellish oaths and perjuries and blasphemies.

entries.title: Psalms 139:21
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t I appeal to thee the omnipresent and omniscient God, whether I do not perfectly hate them so far as they are enemies to God and goodness.

u In open hostility and rebellion against thine Authority.

entries.title: Psalms 139:22
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: x I am no less grieved with their enmity against thee than if they directed it against my self.

entries.title: Psalms 139:23
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Job 31. 6. Psal. 26. 2.

y And whether I do not speak this from my very heart, do thou judge who art the searcher of hearts, and deal with me accordingly.

entries.title: Psalms 139:24
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. way of pain, or, grief.

z Heb. way of trouble or grief, any course of life which is grievous, either 1. to my self, as all sin is to the sinner sooner or later: or, 2. to others; as I am accused of causing much trouble and design[illegible]ng mischief to the King and Kingdom.

Psal. 5. 8. & 143. 10.

a In the right and good way, which is lasting and leads to everlasting life, whereas the way of wickedness, to which this i[illegible]opposed, will perish, as is said Psal. 1. 6. and bring men i[illegible]o utter destruction. Or, as others render it, in the old way, which is the good way, as it is called Ier. 6. 16. in the way of righteousness and holiness, which may well b[illegible] called the old way, because it was from the beginning of the world written in ma[illegible]s heart, whereas wickedness is of a later date. Possibly it may be rendred in thy way (the Ellipsis of the Pronoum being very frequent, as hath been noted and proved before: or, in the way, to w[illegible]t, the way of God, which is oft called emph[illegible]ically the way, as Psal. 25. 8. & 119. 1. Prov. 23. 19. & 29. 27. and which is sufficiently understood from its opposition to the wicked way in the former clause) for ever, or, as long as I live, as this Hebrew word Olam without any prefix to it is used, 2 Sam. 27. 12. Iob 41. 4. Psal. 21. 4. & 45. 7. and elsewhere. But this with submission.

entries.title: Psalms 140:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Either Saul or Doeg or some other malicious enemy, or rather enemies: the word man being taken collectively for men, as appears from the next verse, where he speaks of this man in the Plural number.

Heb. man of violences.

entries.title: Psalms 140:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: b To execute those bloody enterprises which they had devised in the first clause of this verse.

entries.title: Psalms 140:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
c Their malicious hearts stirred up their tongues to utter vile slanders against me.

d Either whetting their tongues as serpents are said to whet theirs when they are about to bite: or rather, using words as sharp and piercing as the sting of a serpent.

Psal. 58. 4 Rom. 3. 13.

entries.title: Psalms 140:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
e Whose design and full resolution it is, if thou dost not prevent it.

f Or, my [illegible]eet or footsteps, i. e. to throw me down to the ground, to defeat all my hopes and counsels, and bring me to ruine.

entries.title: Psalms 140:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 35. 7. & 57. 6. & 141. 9. Jer. 18. 22.

g My in[illegible]olent enemies who despise me for my meanness, and exalt themselves against thee.

Heb. hand.

h In which I used to walk.

entries.title: Psalms 140:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: i With thy powerful protection as with an helmet or shield.

entries.title: Psalms 140:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
k Which is to destroy me.

Or, let them not be exalted.

Deut. 32. 27.

l Not onely against me, but against thee also, as if by their power and policy they had frustrated thy design and promise made to me.

entries.title: Psalms 140:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m Or, beads, the Singular number put for the Plural, as is frequent. By which he understands either, 1. their politick heads, their chiefs or ring-leaders, who were most malicious, and by whom all the rest were supported and stirred up: or, 2. their proper and natural heads, as this word is used v. 7. and this covering of their heads here is opposed to that covering of Davids head there.

Psal. 7. 16. & 94. 23. Prov. 12. 13. & 18. 7.

n Let the mischief which by their calumnies they design against me, fall upon themselves.

entries.title: Psalms 140:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 11. 6.

o Divine vengeance, which is compared to coals of fire, as Psal. 18. 12. and elsewhere.

p Either to my danger, or to their own comfort.

entries.title: Psalms 140:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. a man of tongue.

Or, an evil speaker, a wicked man of violence be established in the [illegible]arth: let him be hunted to his overthrow.

q Such as slander me and other innocent persons, to exasperate Princes against us.

r Either the evil of punishment, or, which comes to the same thing, the evil of sin, their own wickedness, which shall recoil upon themselves.

entries.title: Psalms 140:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: s Both by Gods word which hath promised it, and by my own experience of it in the course of Gods providence.

entries.title: Psalms 140:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t Shall have occasion to praise thee for their deliverance.

u Shall constantly enjoy thy gracious and powerful presence and assistance.

entries.title: Psalms 141:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. directed.

a Heb. Be directed to thy face. Let it not be lost, but let it come unto thee and find audience.

b Owned and accepted by thee no less than the incense, which by thy command, Exod. 30. 7, &c. is offered upon thine Altar, from which I am now banished and so disenabled to offer it there, and therefore I trust thou wilt accept my prayer instead of it.

c My prayer made with hands lifted up, which was the usual gesture. See Iob 11. 13. Psal. 63. 5. & 88. 10, &c.

d Which was offered every evening, Exod. 29. 39, &c. Which he mention[illegible] either, 1. by way of opposition to the incense which was offered in the morning: or, 2. Synecdochically, so as to include the morning-sacrifice and all the sacrifices of the day, of which this was the close; such Synecdoches being most frequent, as hath been already observed: or, 3. because the evening-sacrifice was more solemn than the morning, and was attended with more company and more prayers, whence the ninth hour, which was the time of this sacrifice, is called the hour of prayer, Acts 3. 1.

entries.title: Psalms 141:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
e That I may not through mine own infirmity and the great provocations of mine enemies, break [illegible]orth into any unadvised speeches or any expressions of impa[illegible]ience or distrust or envy or malice, &c.

f My lips which are the door of my mouth whence words come forth.

entries.title: Psalms 141:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
g Suffer it not to be inclined or led aside either by my own errours or lusts, or by the temptations of the world or of the Devil. Thus God is frequently said to harden mens hearts not positively, for he can do no evil, nor tempt any man to it, Iam. 1. 13. but privatively, by denying sof[illegible]ning grace.

h Keep me not onely from wicked speeches, v. 3. but from all evil motions of my heart, which otherwise will draw me to many evil speeches and actions.

i Either, 1. to joyn with them in their sinful courses: or, 2. to do wickedly as they do.

k Let me never enjoy or desire worldly comforts upon such terms as they do, to wit, with Gods wrath and curse, as instruments of wickedness, and of my own eternal destruction. My afflictions are more desirable than such prosperity. Let none of their sweet morsels, the pleasures o[illegible] advantages, which they gain by their wickedness, tempt me to approve of or imitate their ways.

entries.title: Psalms 141:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Prov. 9. 8.

Or, let the righteous smi[illegible] me kindly, and reprove me; let not their precious oil break my head, &c.

l To wit, with his tongue by reproofs, as the next clause explains it, which are called wounds, Prov. 27. 6. As I pray unto thee that [illegible] would[illegible]st keep me from sinful practices, so I beg it of all just men, that if I do transgress, or if, by the arts and slanders of mine enemies, any of them are made to believe that I am guilty of [illegible]il designs against Saul, or of any other wickedness, that they would freely admonish and reprove me for it And their reproofs shall please me better than the dainties of the wicked last mentioned, v. 4.

m I shall be so far from being offended with it as an act of enmity or ill will, as they may suspect, that I shall esteem it an act and sign of true friendship.

n Or, it shall be as the oil of the head, as it is in the Hebrew, i. e. which is poured upon the head, as the manner was in great feasts and solemnities.

o Not hurt or disturb it, but on the contrary, shall heal and greatly refresh and delight it. Which is here understood by a known figure called Meiosis, whereby more is intended than is expressed, as Prov. 17. 21. and oft elsewhere.

p Either, 1. in the calamities of those righteous persons who reproved and censured him. So this is an evidence of what he last said, that he should take their reproofs for a kindness, because when they came into such calamities as those wherein he was involved, as all righteous men must expect sufferings at one time or other, he would not insult over them nor censure them, but pity them and pray for them: or, 2. in the calamities of his enemies, of which he speaks in the next words. And so this may be added as a reason why he did so freely offer himself to the righteous to be reproved by them, if he or his cause were so bad as his enemies made them, because he was well assured that he was sincere and his cause good, and that God would bring him out of all his calamities, and bring his enemies into such calamities, that they should need and desire his prayers, which also he would willingly grant to them; and then all good men would be fully satisfied of the justice of his person and cause.

entries.title: Psalms 141:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
q The chief of mine enemies, their Governors Civil and Military.

r Or, shall be overthrown, or cast down headlong by thine exemplary vengeance. Or, as others, were left free, unhurt by me, when it was in my power to destroy them: of which see 1 Sam. 24. & 26. to which histories this place is by divers learned Interpreters thought to allude. And then by their Iudges he means Saul, although he thought not fit distinctly to mention him, but onely to intimate him in an obscure and general way.

s Heb. in the hands or by the sides of the rock. Which may relate either, 1. to the rocky nature of those places in which Saul fell into Davids hands. See 1 Sam. 24. 2. or, 2. to the ancient manner of punishing malefactors, which was by throwing them down from the tops of rocks: of which see 2 Chron. 25. 12. or, 3. to aggravate their overthrow; for falls in stony places are as most easie and frequent, so also most mischievous.

t Then they, either the Judges, who will be wise too late; or the people spared by my favour, when others were overthrown and warned by that fearful example, will hear my words, i. e. hearken to my counsels and offers which now they despise, and then they, my words, will be sweet and acceptable to them, which now they reject. Others thus, then they did hear my words that they were sweet, then they acknowledged that my words and carriage towards Saul were full of meekness and gentleness, and that I was not so false and malicious, as they had represented me to be.

entries.title: Psalms 141:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
u My bones and the bones of my friends and followers. Our skin and flesh is in a manner consumed, and there is nothing left of us but a company of dead and dry bones. Whereby he intimates that their condition was desperate. Comp. Ezek. 37. 11.

x Either, 1. literally and properly. So barbarously cruel were our enemies, that they not onely killed us, but left our carkasses unburied, by which means our flesh and sinews, &c. were consumed or torn in pieces by wild [illegible]easts, and our bones dispersed upon the face of the earth our common grave: or, if any of my followers were dead and buried, they pulled their bones out of the grave, and scattered them about: or rather, 2. Metaphorically. So the sence is, Our case is almost as hopeless as of those who are dead, and whose bones are scattered in several places.

y As much neglected and despised by them as the chips which a Carpenter makes when he is cutting wood, which he will not stoop to take up. Or rather, as the LXX. and Chaldee and Syriack understand it, and as it is in the Hebrew, as when one (to wit, the husbandman) cutteth and cleaveth the earth or in the earth; which he teareth without any mercy.

entries.title: Psalms 141:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. make [illegible] soul bare, [illegible] [illegible]. [illegible] [illegible]. 5. 2, 3.

z Or, naked, as this word signifies Psal. 137. 7. and a[illegible] Aa[illegible]on is said to have made the people naked, Exod. 32. 25. i. e. deprived of thy favour and protection. Or, do not po[illegible]r out my soal, to wit, unto death, as this word is used, Isa. 53. 12.

entries.title: Psalms 141:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
a Heb. Into his nets, either into Gods nets, the Relative being put without the Antecedent, as is usual in such cases, where it is easily understood. Or, each into his own nets, to wit, the mischiefs which he designs against me.

b Or, together, to wit, with my followers: or, in like manner, as I have d[illegible]e formerly. But this word may seem to be more fitly joyned to the [illegible]oregoing clause, to which it is next placed in the Hebrew, and the verse may be and is by divers both ancient and later Translators, thus rendred, Let the wicked fall (Or, The wicked shall fall) into their own nets together, (altogether, or alik[illegible], one as well as another, Saul himself not excepted, whom though I dare not destroy, God will judge) whilst that I escape, am preserved from that common calamity in which mine enemies shall perish. Which was verified by the event. For David was strangely kept out of harms way when Saul and others of Davids enemies were cut off by the Phisisti[illegible]s, 1 Sam. 31.

Heb pass over.

entries.title: Psalms 142:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: b Either, 1. with the voice of my soul. But so this addition would be superfluous, and much more the repetition of it, because that is necessarily implied in the former word, I cried, and in the following, I make my supplication. Or rather, 2. with my corporeal voice, which the fervor of my soul forced me to use, when I could not do it without some danger, the enemy being at the mouth of the cave. And so this addition is emphatical, and therefore is repeated. But it is probable that David spoke with a low voice, and that he might do so without very great danger, is manifest from that discourse which passed between David and his men, even when Saul was entred into the cave, 1 Sam. 24, 4, 5, 6, 7.

entries.title: Psalms 142:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 102. tit.

c I did it fully and fervently and confidently.

entries.title: Psalms 142:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d To wit, practically, so as to direct me to it.

e What paths I should chuse whereby I might escape Saul, when I fled hither and thither in desarts and mountains and woods; and which way I should get out of his hands when he and all his men were at the caves mouth, which passed my skill.

Psal. 140. 5.

f Wherein I used to walk, or they supposed that I would walk.

entries.title: Psalms 142:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, look on the right hand and see.

g The place where the Patron or Assistant used to stand. See Psal. 16. 8. & 109. 31. & 121. 5.

Psal. 88. 8.

h To wit, in Sauls Court or Camp: none of my former acquaintance and friends and relations.

i Owne me, or shew any respect or kindness to me.

Heb. per[illegible] from me.

Heb. no man sought after [illegible]y soul.

k Or, for my life, to wit, to preserve it; but they all conspired to take it away; which is here implied.

entries.title: Psalms 142:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 16. 5. & 73. 26.

l Thou onely art both my re[illegible]uge to defend me from all evil, and my portion to supply me with all the good which I need and desire.

m Even in this life, wherein I doubt not to see Gods goodness, as he said Psal. 27. 13.

entries.title: Psalms 142:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n Bring me safe out of this cave wherein I am imprisoned, and set me at perfect liberty.

o Shall flock to me from all parts, partly out of curiosity to see such a spectacle and miracle of Gods power and mercy; and partly to rejoyce and bless God with me and for me and for all the benefits which they expect from my government.

entries.title: Psalms 143:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: a Whereby thou art inclined and engaged to favour righteous persons and just causes.

entries.title: Psalms 143:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, but.

b But when I appeal to thy righteousness, I do it onely with respect to mine enemies, whose cause as well as their persons is worse than mine, but not in reference to thee, as if I could absolutely justifie my self upon a severe tryal at the Tribunal of thy Justice; for if thou shouldest rigorously examine all the passages of mine heart and life, I dread the thoughts and consequences of it.

Exod. 34. 7. Job 4. 17. Rom. 3. 20. Gal. 2. 16.

c To wit, upon terms of strict justice, without thy indulgence and infinite mercy.

entries.title: Psalms 143:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d This is not a reason of what he last said, v. 2. but an argument to enforce his petition delivered v. 1. and repeated v. 7, &c. For though I am not faultless, if thou shouldest make an exact search into me, yet mine enemies are more culpable and highly unjust, and therefore I hope for thy help against them from thy justice as well as mercy.

e i. e. My life; for nothing less will satisfie him.

f He hath beaten me down to the ground where I lie strugling for life.

g He hath forced me to have mine abode in dark vaults and caves.

h Where I am out of sight and memory, and in as [illegible]orlorn and hopeless a condition in the eye of man, as those that have [illegible]ain long rotting in the grave.

entries.title: Psalms 143:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i See on Psal. 61. 2. & 14[illegible]. 3.

k Deprived of all hope and comfort. Or, is astonished.

entries.title: Psalms 143:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 77. 5. 11.

l i. e. What thou hast done for thy servants in former times. Which he mentions either, 1. as matter of terror, to consider how unlike God now was to himself and to his former dealings: or, 2. as matter of support from former experience, because God was still the same. Either way it drive him to his prayers, which here follow.

entries.title: Psalms 143:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m I pray to thee [illegible]ervently. See on Psal. 141. 2.

Psal. 63. 1.

n After thy favour and help.

o To wit, thirs[illegible]eth for rain.

entries.title: Psalms 143:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 28. 1.

Or, for I am become like, &c.

p That are dead and buried, of whom there is no hope.

entries.title: Psalms 143:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:

Psal. 25. 1.

s Without whose care these caves and rocks can give me no protection.

entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 25. 4, 5. & 139. 24.

t To continue in faithful obedience to thee, notwithstanding all temp[illegible]ations to the contrary.

u Or rather, as it is exactly in the Hebrew, and as many both ancient and modern Translators render it, Let thy good Spirit lead me. Leave me not to my own blind and vain mind or corrupt affections, neither give me up to the evil Spirit, as thou didst Saul, [illegible]ut conduct me in all my ways by thy good, i. e. gracious and holy Spirit.

x Or, in plain or even land or ground, in a straight and smooth path, that I may not stumble nor fall either into sin or mischief. This is opposed to the crooked and rugged ways in which sinners are said to walk. See Psal. 125. 5. Prov. 2. 15. Isa. 40. 4.

entries.title: Psalms 143:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
y Out of thy mercy to me, whose life they seek.

Psal. 16. 16.

entries.content:
Heb. [illegible]y rock.

[illegible] Sam. 22. [illegible]5.

Heb. to the war, &c.

a Who hast given me that skill in military conduct, and that dexterity in the management of my weapons, which was wholly unsuitable to and much above my education and former course of life.

entries.title: Psalms 144:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
2 Sam. 22. 2, 3, 40. 48.

Or, my mercy.

b Or, my mercy: or, the God of my mercy, as God is called Psal. 59. 10, 17. the Name of God being ea[illegible]ily understood from the foregoing verse. Or, he who is exceeding good or merciful to me, as good as goodness it sel[illegible]: the abstract being put for the concrete, as it is frequently in speeches of God, who is called wisdom, Truth, Goodness, &c. and sometimes of men, as Psal. 12. 2. Prov. 10. 29. where faithfulness and uprightness are put for faithful and upright men.

c Who hast disposed my peoples hearts to receive and obey me as their King.

entries.content:
[illegible]ob 7. 17. Psal. 8. 4. Heb. 2. 6.

d He aggravates Gods goodness to him expressed v. 2. by the consideration of his own meanness. Though I am King over my people, yet al[illegible]s I am but a man, a base, sinful, mortal and miserable creature, if compared with thee, less than nothing and vanity.

e i. e. Hast any care and kindness for him, as words of knowledge commonly imply in Scripture.

f The same thing repeated in other words.

entries.title: Psalms 144:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] 14. 2. [illegible] 39. 5. & [illegible]. 9.

g In his nature and continuance in the world.

h Or, to a vapor or a breath, as Isa. 57. 13. which is gone in an instant.

i Or, that declineth, as Psal. 102. 11. & 109. 23. that groweth less and less till it be quite out of [illegible]ight and lost.

entries.title: Psalms 144:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 18. 9.

k To help me, before it be too late, remembring what a srail and perishing creature I am.

[illegible]. 104. 32.

l Or, that they may smoke: or, and let them smoke, as Sinai did at thy glorious appearance, Exod. 19. 18. This is a figurative and Poetical description of Gods coming to take vengeance upon his enemies, which is continued in the next verse.

entries.title: Psalms 144:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)

[illegible] 18. 13, [illegible]

m Thy thunderbolts which oft accompany the lightnings and thunder.

[illegible]. bands.

n Either of the Heathen nations which envy and hate me: or of the rebellious Israelites, who, though they profess themselves to be the Lords people, yet in truth and for their carriage to me are like the barbarous Heathens.

entries.title: Psalms 144:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o Either, 1. vain brags and threatnings which shall come to nothing: or, 2. vain and deceitful promises or professions of friendship.

p Here mentioned either, 1. as it is used in swearing, to note their perjury: or rather, 2. as an instrument of action.

q Deceiving either, 1. themselves, by being unable to do what they designed: or, 2. others, by not giving them that help which they promised to them.

entries.title: Psalms 144:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 33. 2, 3.

r When thou hast granted this request of mine, v. 7, 8. which I know assuredly thou wilt do.

entries.title: Psalms 144:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] [illegible]ictory.

s Who are not preserved by their own power or prudence, but by Gods special providence, which for the publick good of the world watcheth over them.

entries.title: Psalms 144:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: t And upon these accounts grant me the mercy which [illegible] desired before, and now again do repeat.

entries.title: Psalms 144:12
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
u This mercy I beg not onely for my own sake, but for the sake of thy people, that thine and our enemies being subdued, and peace established in the land, thy people may enjoy those blessings which thou hast promised to them; and particularly, that our sons, which are the strength and safety and hopes of a nation, may be like plants, flourishing and thriving and growing in height and strength, as plants do in their youth, and then onely; for when they grow old, they wither and decay.

x Upon whom the hope of posterity depends.

[illegible] [illegible].

y Strong and beautiful, and adorned with all the ornaments belonging to their sex.

entries.title: Psalms 144:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] from [illegible] [illegible] kind.

z So as they may fill our streets, being brought in thither for food to the Towns and Cities. Or, in our folds or stables, as the Chaldee and others render it; or, as the LXX. and others, in their (or rather, in our, as it is in the Hebrew) outlets or outgoings, i. e. in the fields where they abide.

entries.title: Psalms 144:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. able to bear bardens, or loaden with flesh.

a Heb. laden, either with flesh and [illegible]at, as many understand it: or, as others, with young: but then the foregoing word is not to be rendred oxen, but cows, as the same word and in the same Masculine gender is used Deut. 7. 13. And so this agrees best with the former prayer for the sheep v. 13. and he wisheth the same blessing of fruitfulness both for greater and smaller cattel.

b To wit, of enemies invading the Land, or assaulting our Cities, and making breaches in their walls.

c To wit, of our people, either out of the Towns and Cities to fight with an invading enemy: or out of the Land into captivity.

d Or, no out[illegible]ry, or howling for any sad tidings, or publick grievances or calamities.

entries.title: Psalms 144:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 33. 12 & 65. 4.

e This is a correction of the last sentence. This is a very desirable estate, but the true and chief happiness of our Israel doth not consist in these things, which are common to others with us, but in this peculiar priviledge that the true and blessed God is our God by covenant and special relation.

entries.title: Psalms 145:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, the king. Compare Je[illegible]. 38. 9.

a Or, the King, by way of eminency, the King of kings, the God by whom Kings reign, and to whom I and all other Kings owe subjection and obedience.

entries.title: Psalms 145:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. and of his greatness. there is no search.

Job 5. 9. & 9. 10.

b In his Being, Majesty and Glory, and all Perfections.

entries.title: Psalms 145:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: c The people that live in one age shall relate them to their posterity, and so successively in all ages.

entries.title: Psalms 145:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d Here are divers words heaped together to intimate that no words were sufficient to express it.

Heb. things, or, words.

entries.title: Psalms 145:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: Heb. declare it.

entries.title: Psalms 145:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. [illegible].

e The memorials of thy kindness to thy people, thy never to be forgotten blessings.

entries.title: Psalms 145:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Exod. 34 6, 7. Numb. 14. 18. Psal. 86. 5, 15. & 103. 8.

Heb. great in mercy.

entries.title: Psalms 145:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: f Not to Israel onely, but to all mankind, whose hearts he fills with food and gladness, as it is said Acts 14. 17. yea to all his creatures, as it is in the next clause, to beasts, as well as men. See Psal. 39. 6. and 147. 9.

entries.title: Psalms 145:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: g Objectively, they give men and Angels just occasion to praise thee.

entries.title: Psalms 145:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: Heb. a kingdom of all ages.

entries.title: Psalms 145:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
h Either, 1. all that look up to him for help: or, 2. all that are upheld: whose support is not from themselves, nor from other men, but onely from Gods powerful and good providence.

Psal. 146. 8.

entries.title: Psalms 145:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i Of all living creatures.

Or, look unto thee.

k Expect and receive their supplies wholly from thy bounty. Expectation is here figuratively ascribed to brute creatures, as Psal. 104. 27. Rom. 8. 22.

Psal. 136. 25.

l When they need it.

entries.title: Psalms 145:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: m Or, as divers render it, and which is more agreeable to the order of the words in the Hebrew Text, thou satisfiest every living thing with thy favour or good-will, i. e. with the fruits of thy bounty: the Pronoun thy being easily and fitly understood out of the foregoing clause.

entries.title: Psalms 145:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Or, merciful, or, bountiful.

n Or rather merciful, as this word most commonly signifies. There is a mixture of mercy in the most severe and terrible works of God in this life, judgment without mercy being reserved for the next life, Iam. 2. 13. Revel. 14. 10.

entries.title: Psalms 145:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Deut. 4. 7.

o To answer their prayers for relief.

p Sincerely or with an upright heart, trusting to him, and waiting upon him in his way.

entries.title: Psalms 145:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: q So far as it is agreeable to his own will, and convenient for their good; not inordinate desires, which God commonly denies to his people in mercy, and granteth to his enemies in anger.

entries.title: Psalms 145:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: r Frequently in this world, but infallibly in the next.

entries.title: Psalms 146:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: Heb. Hallelujah.

entries.title: Psalms 146:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 118. 8. 9.

a In men of greatest wealth and power, in whose favour men are very prone to trust.

Or, salvation.

b Who are utterly unable frequently to give you that help which they promise, and you expect.

entries.title: Psalms 146:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 104. 29. Eccl. 12. 7.

Heb. spirit. So Gr.

c In his body, Eccles. 12. 7.

d To that earth from which all mankind, Princes not excepted, had their original.

e As soon as ever he is dead.

f All his designs and endeavours either for himself or for others.

entries.title: Psalms 146:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Gen. 1. 1.

g Both because he liveth for ever to fulfil his promises, and because he is eternally and unchangeably faithful.

entries.title: Psalms 146:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Mat. 9. 30. John 9. 7 32.

h Either, 1. the eyes of their mind, which he enlightens and directs in doubtful and difficult cases: or, 2. their bodily eyes; which he did abundantly by his Son Jesus Christ.

Psal. 145. 14. Luke 13. 13.

i Even when he doth afflict them, which also he doth out of love, Heb. 12. 6.

entries.title: Psalms 146:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Deut. 10. 18. Psal. 68. 5.

k He overthroweth their goings, as the phrase is Psal. 140. 4. He maketh them to lose their way; he not onely frustrateth their plots and enterprises, but turneth them against themselves. This and all the foregoing sentences are so many arguments to encourage all good men to trust in God in all their straits and afflictions.

entries.title: Psalms 147:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal 92. 1[illegible]

a It is acceptable to God, and greatly comfortable and beneficial to our selves.

Psal. 33. 1.

entries.content:
b It is the Lords own doing, and not mans.

Deut. 30. 3.

c Or, the banished, who were carried captives out of their own land, and dispersed in divers strange countries.

entries.title: Psalms 147:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
d Either with the sence of their sins: or with their sorrows and grievous calamities. He seems to speak peculiarly of the captive Israelites now returned.

Heb. griess.

entries.title: Psalms 147:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Isa. 40. 26.

e Which no man can do, Gen. 22. 17. For those thousand and twenty five which Astronomers number, are onely such as are most distinctly visible to the eye, and most considerable for their influences.

f This signifies, 1. that he exactly knows them as we do those whom we can call by name; he is able to give distinct names to each of them, because he accurately understands their several natures and operations: 2. That he hath a Soveraign power over them, as men have over their children or servants or souldiers whom they can call by name, that he appointeth and governeth all their motions and influences to the fulfilling of his own pleasure and purposes.

entries.title: Psalms 147:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: Heb. of his understanding there is no number.

entries.title: Psalms 147:8
