[illegible] [illegible]5. 15.

[illegible], [illegible]. Job 38. 4.

g Which he mentions partly because they were most contemptible, especially to the Jews, to whom they were unclean and forbidden for food: partly because they are greedy and voracious: and partly because they are not onely neglected by men, but also forsaken by their dams as soon as ever they can flie, and so are wholly left to the care and keeping of Divine providence.

entries.title: Psalms 147:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. 33. 16. [illegible] 1. 7.

h As if he needed either the one or the other for the accomplishment of his designs.

entries.title: Psalms 147:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: i That believingly and patiently expect and seek relief and happiness from God alone, and from his meer grace and mercy, and not from any creature, nor from their own merits.

entries.title: Psalms 147:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: k Thy strength consists not in thy walls and gates and bars, but in his protection.

entries.title: Psalms 147:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. who [illegible] thy bor [illegible] [illegible].

l In all thy land, even to its utmost borders, which are most liable to the incursion of enemies.

[illegible] 132. 15.

[illegible] [illegible]at of [illegible]. [illegible] [illegible]. 16.

entries.title: Psalms 147:15
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
m Which is sufficient without any instruments to execute whatsoever pleaseth him, either in works of nature or of providence.

n The thing is done without delay or difficulty.

entries.title: Psalms 147:16
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
o Not onely in colour and shape and softness, but also in use, keeping the fruits of the earth warm.

p In colour and smalness of parts, as also in its burning quality.

entries.title: Psalms 147:17
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
q Either, 1. pieces of ice, which God may be said to cast forth or to cast down, because he sendeth it, and oft-times suddenly: or, 2. great hail-stones, which are of an icy nature and substance, and which are very properly cast forth or cast down out of the clouds, and that like morsels or fragments, the particles being congealed in them.

r The cold which he sometimes sends into the air is so sharp, that it would be intolerable, if men did not defend themselves from it by houses, cloaths, fire, &c.

entries.title: Psalms 147:18
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. spirit. [illegible] 40. 7.

s The Southern or some other warm wind sent with commission to dissolve the ice.

t The rivers return to their course which before were bound up by, or turned into, ice.

entries.title: Psalms 147:19
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. his [illegible].

u He fully declared his mind and will by revelation and in his word.

x To the children of Iacob or Israel, and to them alone, as it follows.

entries.title: Psalms 147:20
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible] Rom 3. 42.

y He left all others to their own native darkness and blindness, and to those dim discoveries of God and of themselves which they had from the light of Nature.

entries.title: Psalms 148:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
[illegible]. Hallelu [illegible]

a All the host of Heaven, which he particularly expresseth in the following verses.

b In those high and heavenly places.

entries.title: Psalms 148:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 103. 20, 21.

c He inviteth the Angels here, and the senseless creatures afterward, to praise God, not as if the former needed, or the latter were capable of, his exhortation, but onely by a Poetical rapture, the design whereof is, that men by this means might be more provoked to this duty.

d The Angels, called hosts, here and 1 Kings 22. 19. for their vast numbers, exquisite order, and perfect subjection to their General, the Lord of hosts.

entries.title: Psalms 148:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: e You which are adored by the blind Heathens for gods, you are but his creatures, and therefore were obliged, if you were capable, to worship and praise him for your glorious light and powerful influences.

entries.title: Psalms 148:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
f Ye highest and most glorious Heavens, the place of Gods Throne and glorious presence, as this phrase is used, Deut. 10. 14. 1 Kings. 8. 27. Neh. 9. 6. Psal. 115. 16. Or ye starry Heavens, which also may well be so called, because they are above the air, which is oft called Heaven in Scripture.

g Ye clouds which are above a part of the Heavens. Of which see on Gen. 1. 7.

entries.title: Psalms 148:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Gen. 1. 1, 6. Psal. 33. 9.

h They owe their being wholly to Gods good will.

entries.title: Psalms 148:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 89. 37. & 119. 90, 91. Jer. 31. 35, 36.

i Either absolutely as to the substance of them, or at least to the end of the world. He hath made them constant and incorruptible, not changeable and perishing, as the things of the lower world are.

k Either concerning their several courses and influences: or rather for their continuance for ever; which best agrees with the foregoing and following words.

l Which decree shall never be made void.

entries.title: Psalms 148:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: m Either, 1. dragons and serpents, which abide in the deep caverns and holes of the earth: or, 2. whales or other Sea-monsters, which dwell in the depths of the Sea, which are oft called by this name, as Iob 7. 12. Ezek. 29. 3. and elsewhere, as the word here rendred deeps is most commonly used concerning the Sea.

entries.title: Psalms 148:8
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
n Lightnings and other fire-works of the air.

o Or, sumes, hot exhalations, as the word properly signifies, as cold exhalations are comprehended under the title of snow. And both of them arising from the earth, are here fitly mentioned as belonging to it.

p Executing his commands either for the comfort and refreshment, or for the punishment, of the inhabitants of the earth.

entries.title: Psalms 148:9
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: q Admirable for your height and strength and use, though not for your fruit.

entries.title: Psalms 148:10
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: Heb. birds of wing.

entries.title: Psalms 148:11
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: r Who, though you are called gods, and adored like gods by your Subjects, yet are but men, and the creatures and Subjects of this Soveraign Lord, to whom you owe both your being, and all your power and dignity.

entries.title: Psalms 148:13
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 8. 1. Isai. 12. 4.

Heb. exalted.

s Not so much in place as in excellency, above all the glories which are in earth and in Heaven.

entries.title: Psalms 148:14
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
t To wit, above the horns of all the people in the world, in respect of their spiritual and eternal priviledges, as it here follows. The born in Scripture doth commonly note strength, victory, glory and felicity, as Deut. 33. 17. and every where.

u Either, 1. He is the praise, as God is called Deut. 10. 21. to wit, the God of their praise, as Psal. 109. 1. the chiefest object and matter of it: or, 2. which is the praise. Which work of God in exalting their horn is their glory, and maketh them praise-worthy, or obligeth and provoketh them in a singular manner to perform this great duty of praising God, which is so generally neglected by others.

x By special relation and friendship and covenant, and by familiar intercourses, God manifesting his face and favour to them, and they frequently and solemnly approaching into his presence, and worshipping him at his footstool.

entries.title: Psalms 149:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. Hallelujah.

Psal. 33. 3.

a For these new mercies conferred upon us, denied to former times.

entries.title: Psalms 149:2
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 100. 3.

b That made them not onely his creatures, but, which is unspeakably greater, his people: or, that advanced and adorned them with singular priviledges, as this word is used, 1 Sam. 12. 6. and elsewhere.

c David and his posterity, and especially the chief of all of them, the Messiah. Let them rejoyce and bless God that they have so potent, so wise, and so just a King.

entries.title: Psalms 149:3
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Psal. 81. 2.

Or, with the pipe.

d According to the usage of that time and dispensation.

entries.title: Psalms 149:4
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
e He loveth them above all people, and rejoyceth over them to do them good.

f Heb. adorn or glorifie, make them amiable and honourable in the eyes of the world, who now hate and despise them.

g Or, humble, to wit, his people, as he now said, who are oft in Scripture described by that character, because all true Israelites are such, and all Israelites profess and ought to be such. Or, the afflicted, as that word is oft used in Scripture, which hath been observed before, his poor afflicted and oppressed people, to whom the following salvation is most needful and acceptable.

h Both temporal, in delivering them from, and setting them above, all their enemies, and afterwards, with everlasting salvation and glory.

entries.title: Psalms 149:5
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
i For the honour which God putteth upon them.

k Either, 1. for their safe and sweet repose and peace, which is signified by resting in beds, Isa. 57. 2. or, 2. by night as well as by day, even in the time devoted to rest and sleep, which they shall borrow to praise God for his eminent and extraordinary blessings, as David frequently did upon such occasions.

entries.title: Psalms 149:6
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. the exaltations.

Heb. in their throat.

l Heb. in their throat. Which signifies vocal praise, and that with a loud voice.

Heb. 4. 12. Rev. 1. 16.

m Not onely to defend themselves from their enemies, but, as it follows, to revenge themselves upon them.

entries.title: Psalms 149:7
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content: n For all their cruelties and injuries towards Gods people. This was literally accomplished by David upon the Philistines, Ammonites, Syrians, and other neighbouring Nations and Princes, which were bitter enemies to Gods people. And the same thing was done afterward in the Christian world, when God raised up Christian Princes, who did by the help of the Christians fighting with and under them, severely revenge the blood of the martyred Christians upon their cruel Persecutors and Tyrants in divers ages. It may also be understood of the spiritual plagues which Christ by the hand or ministry of his Apostles and Ministers did inflict upon the hearts and consciences of his incorrigible enemies, who by Gods word and ordinances were either tormented or hardned to their destruction. Yea it may have a respect unto the last day of judgment, in which the Saints shall judge the world, 1 Cor. 6. 2. which will be a most dreadful execution of this vengeance, &c.

Deut. 7. 1, 2.

p Appointed and declared in the holy Scripture, as Deut. 12. 32. & 29. 19. & 32. 41, 42, 43. and elsewhere. This is added to shew that they do not this work to satisfie their own malicious or revengeful inclinations, but in obedience to Gods commands, and onely in such manner as God hath allowed in his word.

q The honour of these actions belongs to all the Saints, for whose sakes God appointed this in his word, and afterwards executed it by his providence.

entries.title: Psalms 150:1
entries.author: Matthew Poole (1624–1679)
entries.content:
Heb. Hallelujah.

a In his Temple, where this work was to be performed constantly and solemnly. Or, who dwelleth in his Sanctuary, So it describeth and limiteth the object of their praises. Or. for (as this particle is used in the next verse) his Sanctuary, for this great favour of placing his Sanctuary and dwelling place amongst men.

b In his heavenly mansion, there let the blessed Angels praise him. Or, who dwelleth in the firmament, or spreading forth of his power, to wit, in the Heavens which were stretched out by his great power, and in which are the most glorious testimonies of his infinite power. Or, for the firmament, &c. for that glorious and astonishing piece of his workmanship.
